title: The darkness within?
caption: The galaxy Messier 85, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 85 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 50 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Messier 85 appears soft and hazy in this Hubble image. It lies around 50 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices, Berenice's Hair, and was first discovered by Pierre Méchain, a colleague of Charles Messier, in 1781.
Its properties sit partway between a lenticular and an elliptical galaxy, and it seems to be interacting with two neighbours out of frame, the spiral NGC 4394 and the small elliptical MCG 3-32-38.

It holds some 400 billion stars, most very old. But its centre hosts relatively young stars only a few billion years old, believed to be the product of a late burst of star birth, probably sparked by a merger with another galaxy more than four billion years ago. And while almost every galaxy is thought to host a supermassive black hole, star motions leave it unclear whether this one does.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.55 x 2.69 arcminutes) and distance (50 million light years), the frame spans roughly 37,000 × 39,000 light-years. Its light set out about 50 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared observations. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Parts of this data are ultraviolet and near-infrared light, both invisible to the eye.
